newsitem.title: USA: Foes of milk hormone win right to label products.
newsitem.headline: Foes of milk hormone win right to label products.

text.p: A group of natural food companies said on Thursday they have won the right under a lawsuit settlement to label their products as free of a synthetic milk hormone.
Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc., the ice cream company based in Burlington, Vt., said the settlement will open the way for companies to use the disclaimers across the United States.

In May 1996, Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc. and other companies sued the state of Illinois and the city of Chicago, seeking the right to label their products as free of milk from cows treated with the growth hormone rBGH.
Illinois was one of four states that did not allow dairy products to be labeled "rBGH free" because, health officials said, there is no way to prove or disprove such a claim.

"We oppose recombinant bovine growth hormone. The family farmers who supply our milk and cream pledge not to treat their cows with rBGH. The FDA has said no significant difference has been shown and no test can now distinguish between milk with rBGH treated and untreated cows."
The controversial hormone made by St. Louis-based Monsanto Co. is genetically engineered to boost milk production in cows. It received federal approval in 1993.
Some critics have charged that it was not adequately tested, could increase the risk of infection in the animals and posed a potential hazard to humans.

Tom Schafer, a spokesman for the Illinois Public Health Department, said the state agreed to the settlement because the companies still will not be able to claim the products are "free" of the hormone -- only that their suppliers have pledged not to use it.

He also said the state was pleased with a second provision that will require labels to state that certain ingredients are contained in the product, such as milk chocolate, and that "Not all suppliers of our other ingredients can promise that the milk they use comes from untreated cows."
A spokeswoman for Ben & Jerry's said the agreement appears to overcome objections from other states that had bans limiting labeling in the area.
The company said it had been unable to use any rBGH labeling claims nationwide because Illinois was such a large market and it could not afford to produce products with two sets of labels.

Other companies involved in the suit were Stonyfield Farm Inc. of Londonderry, N.H.; Whole Foods Market Inc., a group of natural food supermarkets based in Austin, Texas; and Organic Valley, a farmer's cooperative based in La Farge, Wis.
